transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Yeah… um, I guess the main reason I came in is because I’ve been having these thoughts that scare me a little. Not like I’ve made some plan or anything—I haven’t. I haven’t decided to hurt myself. But I keep catching myself thinking, you know, maybe it would just be easier if I didn’t wake up. Like if I could just not have to face everything for a while, or at all, I guess.

It’s not something I’m proud of saying out loud. I’m 54, I work retail, I’m used to just pushing through things and showing up, and I don’t usually talk like this. But the thoughts have been coming up enough that I figured I probably shouldn’t just keep it to myself and pretend it’s nothing.
Did something specific happen in your life around the time these thoughts started?

Yeah. I mean, the big thing was I got fired. That was kind of the start of it, or at least that’s when I noticed things really shifting.

And the weird part is, right after it happened, I didn’t just feel crushed like you’d expect. I felt… fired up, almost. Like, “Fine, I’ll show them. I’ll prove everybody wrong.” I had all this energy around it, like I was going to turn it into something, like they’d made some huge mistake letting me go.

But at the same time, I was really on edge. I remember going to the coffee shop and just snapping at people over stupid little things—like the line moving too slow, or someone standing too close, or the barista not hearing my order right the first time. Stuff that normally might annoy me a little, but I wouldn’t actually say anything. I was just irritated, like everything and everyone was in my way. So yeah, getting fired was definitely the thing that happened around then.
Around that time after you got fired, were you needing less sleep than usual?

Yeah, I was. That was one of the stranger parts, honestly, because normally if I don’t sleep, I feel it the next day. I’m dragging, I’m cranky, I need coffee just to function.

But around then, there were several nights where I only slept maybe two or three hours, and I’d get up feeling like I’d slept plenty. Like I had a full tank, like there was no reason to slow down or go back to bed. I remember thinking, “Well, I’m awake, might as well get going,” and it didn’t seem to catch up with me right away the way it usually would. It felt unusual, looking back.
During that period after you were fired, did you find yourself starting a lot of new projects or being unusually driven to get things done?

Yeah, definitely. I mean, not in a very organized way, looking back, but at the time it felt like I was being productive.

I was bouncing all over the place—one minute I’d be filling out job applications, then I’d stop halfway through and start rewriting my resume because I suddenly decided the whole thing was wrong, then I’d get this idea that maybe I should do something with my hands, like woodworking, and I’d be sketching out little plans for shelves or tables or whatever. I don’t even know why that felt urgent, but it did.

And I wasn’t really sitting still long enough to finish one thing before I’d jump to the next. It was like every idea felt important right then, like if I didn’t act on it immediately I was wasting time. At the time I told myself, “Well, I’m just trying to get back on my feet,” but it was more frantic than that, I think.
During that time after you were fired, did you feel unusually confident or powerful, like you could do things other people couldn’t?

Yeah… I did. I mean, at the time I wouldn’t have called it “powerful,” exactly, but there was definitely this feeling like I knew better than everybody else all of a sudden.

Like, after I got fired, instead of thinking, “Maybe I messed up” or “Maybe I need to figure out what went wrong,” I started thinking, “Honestly, I could walk into any store in this whole district and run it better than the people they have in charge.” And I really believed that for a while. It wasn’t just me blowing off steam, like people do when they’re angry. It felt obvious to me, like I had some kind of clear vision they didn’t have.

I remember looking at other stores, even just walking past them or going in to buy something, and I’d be judging everything—the displays, the staff, the checkout line, how the manager was handling people—and thinking, “I could fix this in a week.” Like losing my job somehow made me the expert on how all of it should be done. Looking back, that seems pretty over the top, but in the moment I felt completely sure of it.
During that period after you were fired, did your behavior get you into serious trouble or make it hard for you to function day to day?

Yeah… it did. I mean, I didn’t end up in some big legal trouble or anything like that, but day-to-day, things started slipping in a way that wasn’t normal for me.

I was supposed to be looking for work, obviously, because I needed a paycheck, but I couldn’t keep it steady. I’d start applications and then not finish them, or I’d miss callbacks because I didn’t check my messages at the right time, or I’d forget an appointment I had set up. Then later I’d realize, “That was important, why didn’t I handle that?” And bills started piling up too. Not because I didn’t care, but because I wasn’t tracking things the way I normally would. I’d think, “I’ll deal with that tonight,” and then I’d get pulled into something else and it just wouldn’t happen.

Even around the house, my routines got sloppy. Laundry, dishes, mail, keeping things organized—stuff I usually can manage even if I’m stressed. It all started to feel scattered. And I remember having this uncomfortable moment where I thought, “Okay, I’m not just being lazy here, and I can’t just snap myself back into order by willpower.” That scared me a little, because I’m used to pushing through things, but this felt like I couldn’t keep a normal rhythm going.
During that period after you were fired, were you talking more than usual or feeling like you couldn’t stop talking?

Yeah, I was talking a lot more than usual. I didn’t really notice it at first, because in my head I was just explaining things, you know? Like I had all these ideas and I needed people to understand the full picture.

I remember sitting at the chess table—there’s a group of guys I’d play with—and I’d start telling them about my plan to come back after getting fired, how I was going to turn things around, what I was going to do next, how I had it all figured out. And once I got going, it was like the words just kept coming. I’d be explaining one part, then another part would pop into my head, and then I’d have to explain that too.

A couple of them actually told me, “Hey, take a breath,” or kind of laughed and said I was talking too fast. At the time I was annoyed, like, “No, you’re not getting it, let me finish.” But looking back, yeah, I think I was kind of hard to interrupt. It felt like if I didn’t get it all out right then, I’d lose the thread or people wouldn’t understand how important it was.
About how long did that fired-up period last?

It lasted… I’d say about three weeks. Maybe not every single hour of every day at the exact same level, but that fired-up, out-of-control feeling was really there for around three weeks after I got fired.

At first I thought it was just adrenaline or anger, like anyone would feel after losing a job, but it didn’t settle down after a day or two. It kept going. And looking back, that’s what stands out to me — it wasn’t just a bad weekend or me being upset for a few days. It was more like this whole stretch where I was running on that intensity, and it took about three weeks before it started to come down.
After that three-week fired-up period ended, did you then go into a stretch where you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Yeah… yes. After that burst of energy wore off, it was like somebody had pulled the plug on me. I don’t even mean just tired like I needed a nap. It was more like everything inside me went flat.

I’d sit at the kitchen table with my coffee in the morning and just stare at it. Not really drinking it, not really thinking clearly either—just sitting there feeling empty. And ashamed, too. That was a big part of it. I kept thinking about how I had acted, how things had gotten away from me, and I just felt this heavy embarrassment, like I didn’t know what to do with myself.

It wasn’t just one bad morning. It kind of settled over me most of the day, day after day. Like the energy was gone and what was left was this hollow feeling.
How long did that depressed stretch last?

It’s been about three months now, I think. Since that crash after the fired-up period ended, the low part has just kind of… stayed.

I kept expecting it to lift after a week or two, like maybe I just needed to rest or get my head straight, but it didn’t really go away. It’s been hanging on for roughly three months, most days feeling like I’m still under it.
During these past three months, have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

Yeah… I have. That’s actually been one of the stranger parts, because the stuff I usually lean on to kind of steady myself just doesn’t do anything for me right now.

Like fishing — normally I can get up early, pack my gear, be out by the water, and even if I don’t catch much, it settles me down. But lately I’ll look at the rods or think about getting everything together and it just feels like work. Same with digging through my vinyl records. I used to be able to spend half an afternoon looking through albums, cleaning one off, putting it on, reading the sleeve notes… now I’ll stand there in front of them and feel nothing, like I’m looking at somebody else’s collection.

Even tailgating, which I used to really enjoy — the food, talking with people, the whole routine — I just don’t care. And I home-brew a little, or I did, and even checking on that has started to feel like another chore I’m failing at instead of something I look forward to.

So yeah, I’d say I lost interest. It’s not that I decided to stop liking those things. They just kind of went flat on me.
